title: Predicting the impact of patient and private provider behavior on diagnostic delay for pulmonary tuberculosis patients in India: A simulation modeling study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis (TB) incidence in India continues to be high due, in large part, to long delays experienced by patients before successful diagnosis and treatment initiation, especially in the private sector. This diagnostic delay is driven by patients' inclination to switch between different types of providers and providers' inclination to delay ordering of accurate diagnostic tests relevant to TB. Our objective is to quantify the impact of changes in these behavioral characteristics of providers and patients on diagnostic delay experienced by pulmonary TB patients. METHODS AND FINDINGS: We developed a discrete event simulation model of patients' diagnostic pathways that captures key behavioral characteristics of providers (time to order a test) and patients (time to switch to another provider). We used an expectation-maximization algorithm to estimate the parameters underlying these behavioral characteristics, with quantitative data encoded from detailed interviews of 76 and 64 pulmonary TB patients in the 2 Indian cities of Mumbai and Patna, respectively, which were conducted between April and August 2014. We employed the estimated model to simulate different counterfactual scenarios of diagnostic pathways under altered behavioral characteristics of providers and patients to predict their potential impact on the diagnostic delay. Private healthcare providers including chemists were the first point of contact for the majority of TB patients in Mumbai (70%) and Patna (94%). In Mumbai, 45% of TB patients first approached less-than-fully-qualified providers (LTFQs), who take 28.71 days on average for diagnosis. About 61% of these patients switched to other providers without a diagnosis. Our model estimates that immediate testing for TB by LTFQs at the first visit (at the current level of diagnostic accuracy) could reduce the average diagnostic delay from 35.53 days (95% CI: 34.60, 36.46) to 18.72 days (95% CI: 18.01, 19.43). In Patna, 61% of TB patients first approached fully qualified providers (FQs), who take 9.74 days on average for diagnosis. Similarly, immediate testing by FQs at the first visit (at the current level of diagnostic accuracy) could reduce the average diagnostic delay from 23.39 days (95% CI: 22.77, 24.02) to 11.16 days (95% CI: 10.52, 11.81). Improving the diagnostic accuracy of providers per se, without reducing the time to testing, was not predicted to lead to any reduction in diagnostic delay. Our study was limited because of its restricted geographic scope, small sample size, and possible recall bias, which are typically associated with studies of patient pathways using patient interviews. CONCLUSIONS: In this study, we found that encouraging private providers to order definitive TB diagnostic tests earlier during patient consultation may have substantial impact on reducing diagnostic delay in these urban Indian settings. These results should be combined with disease transmission models to predict the impact of changes in provider behavior on TB incidence.

summary.oneLiner: Encouraging private providers to order diagnostic tests earlier, rather than focusing solely on diagnostic accuracy, significantly reduces tuberculosis diagnostic delays in India.
summary.overview: In India, many patients with tuberculosis experience long delays before receiving a correct diagnosis because they switch between multiple healthcare providers. This study used a simulation model to understand how patient switching and provider behavior affect these delays. The findings suggest that the most effective way to reduce diagnostic delay is to encourage providers to order tests earlier in the consultation process. Interestingly, the model indicates that simply increasing the diagnostic accuracy of tests—without changing the speed at which providers order them—would not lead to a meaningful reduction in the time it takes to get diagnosed.
summary.question: What is the impact of changing the behavioral characteristics of patients (switching providers) and private healthcare providers (time to ordering diagnostic tests) on diagnostic delays for pulmonary tuberculosis patients in India?
summary.method: The authors developed a discrete event simulation model—a computer-based method for modeling the behavior of complex systems over time—to represent patient pathways. They used an expectation-maximization algorithm to estimate model parameters based on patient interview data.
summary.data: The study used data from detailed, coded interviews with 76 pulmonary tuberculosis patients in Mumbai and 64 in Patna, conducted between April and August 2014.
findings: The study suggests that immediate test ordering by less-than-fully-qualified providers in Mumbai could reduce the average diagnostic delay from 35.53 days to 18.72 days.
The model estimates that immediate test ordering by fully qualified providers in Patna could reduce the average diagnostic delay from 23.39 days to 11.16 days.
Improving diagnostic accuracy of providers, without simultaneously reducing the time to test ordering, is not predicted to lead to any reduction in diagnostic delay.
summary.whyItMatters: The findings suggest that public health interventions should prioritize incentivizing private providers to adopt early testing practices, rather than focusing exclusively on the deployment of high-tech, more accurate diagnostic tools, to reduce diagnostic delays and curb disease transmission.
